segments.expected: "I've six circuits and a month," said Coombe. "I've given this one twelve days. The other five have sent a four to the coast in living memory, and you haven't, in eleven years, and the Board thinks you'll drown." She turned to the cage. "So. A pack."

segments.expected: She did it by laying her palm flat on the grey ward and drawing it aside, as one draws back a curtain, and the ward came away from one end of the box in a single heavy fold and hung there from her hand. It did not tremble. Kiva had seen wards held by Torches, and by Doran Mace's whole line at once, and by Anwen at the end of a long wall with her teeth set. She had never seen one held as this was, by one hand, without the least sign that it was being held at all.

segments.expected: They were husks. Kiva had seen husks since she was thirteen, and these were like all the others and not like any of them. Each was the height of a tall man, a column of grey stuff like a sack of fine ash stood on end, belted at the middle by a knot as thick as a man's arm. Each stood on three thin legs, set wide, like a milking stool. They had no faces. They had a breath, which came out of them all over, as frost comes off a field at dawn, and wherever the breath touched the cinder it went white.

segments.expected: Kiva knew the Pit, as everybody on that rail knew it. It was a floor of packed cinder forty paces by twenty, with a stone race running the length of its south side and a lattice of black iron across the north end, where the Wren House kept what it kept. In the spring she had stood on that cinder for a Flask qualifier with her heart in her mouth, and in the autumn there had been a square of skinned husks over the race with a white cord between them. There was a sixty-year-old mast on the gallery and a rail of worn oak round the top, and the steps down were steep and narrow and slick in frost.
